SAFE: Stepwise Atomic Feedback for Error correction in Multi-hop Reasoning

Daeyong Kwon Email: daeyongkwon@snu.ac.kr    Soyoung Yoon Email: soyoung.yoon@snu.ac.kr Affiliation: Seoul National University, South Korea    Seung-won Hwang ††thanks: Corresponding author Email: seungwonh@snu.ac.kr
Abstract

Multi-hop QA benchmarks frequently reward Large Language Models (LLMs) for spurious correctness, masking ungrounded or flawed reasoning steps. To shift toward rigorous reasoning, we propose SAFE, a dynamic benchmarking framework that replaces the ungrounded Chain-of-Thought (CoT) with a strictly verifiable sequence of grounded entities. Our framework operates across two phases: (1) train-time verification, where we establish an atomic error taxonomy and a Knowledge Graph (KG)-grounded verification pipeline to eliminate noisy supervision in standard benchmarks, identifying up to 14% of instances as unanswerable, and (2) inference-time verification, where a feedback model trained on this verified dataset dynamically detects ungrounded steps in real-time. Experimental results demonstrate that SAFE not only exposes the critical flaws of existing benchmarks at train-time, but also significantly outperforms standard baselines, achieving an average accuracy gain of 8.4 pp while guaranteeing verifiable trajectories at inference-time.11 1 Code and verified benchmarks will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

1 Introduction

The frontier of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted towards complex reasoning, such as multi-hop question answering (QA), requiring models to synthesize evidence across multiple documents to derive a final answer. While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has substantially improved performance on these tasks (Wei et al., 2022), their reasoning traces are hard to ground or verify Turpin et al. (2023). For example, intermediate steps may contain unverified entities, unsupported relations, or implicit shortcuts that nevertheless lead to the correct answer.

Our goal is to make reasoning traces verifiable and thus eliminate spurious reasoning, by shifting from free-form thought generation to rigorous traversal using Knowledge Graph (KG). Specifically, we formalize the reasoning process as a verifiable sequence of grounded entities, subject to the following strict requirements: (1) each step must be atomic, corresponding to a single valid KG triple; (2) all entities must be explicitly anchored in the provided context; and (3) every relation must be independently explainable and verifiable.

To rigorously enforce these grounding constraints on both train-time and inference-time, we build a dynamic benchmarking framework. For train-time verification, we execute two critical offline steps. First, we apply the above strict constraints to verify standard multi-hop benchmarks (Ho et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018; Trivedi et al., 2022), where we remove up to 14% of noisy instances. Second, we formalize an atomic error taxonomy to construct targeted supervision signals for training an external feedback model. At inference-time, this model dynamically verifies each atomic step of the multi-hop reasoning process, detecting and correcting any deviation from a valid KG path on-the-fly. Compared with LLM self-correction which is inherently error-prone (Huang et al., 2023; Tyen et al., 2024), this inference-time verification ensures strictly grounded reasoning trajectories. Collectively, these train-time and inference-time phases constitute SAFE, a dynamic benchmarking framework.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose a train-time verification pipeline to filter noise from standard benchmarks, and define an error taxonomy to construct targeted training signals.

  • •

    We develop an inference-time verification mechanism using a trained feedback model to detect and rectify reasoning deviations in real-time.

  • •

    We introduce SAFE, a novel dynamic benchmarking framework that significantly outperforms baselines with an average +8.4 pp accuracy gain.

2 Related Works

2.1 Multi-hop QA Benchmarks and Spurious Reasoning

Multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022) have been widely adopted for complex reasoning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) evaluation (Jimenez Gutierrez et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2023). However, Ishii et al. (2024) report that a non-trivial portion of correct answers on standard multi-hop QA datasets are spurious.

To reduce spurious reasoning, KG has been used before (Fang et al., 2024) and after generation Nguyen et al. (2024). The former extracts the KG chain before generation and the latter evaluates CoT reasoning by mapping the generated steps to a KG. Closest to our work is REVEAL Jacovi et al. (2024), a benchmark that assigns correctness labels to individual reasoning steps based on a specialized error taxonomy. Hop, Skip, and Overthink (Yadav et al., 2025) is another post-hoc evaluation, curating failure modes to localize breakdowns.

Our distinction: Unlike these post-hoc approaches that focus on error diagnosis after a full trajectory is produced, SAFE diagnoses such errors during generation at inference-time and prevents them at train-time.

2.2 Inference-Time Reasoning Feedback

LLMs can be prompted to critique and revise their own outputs (Madaan et al., 2023) or accumulate reflective feedback across trials (Shinn et al., 2023). Approaches like Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) demonstrate the appeal of self-critique as a mechanism for improving output quality without requiring additional training or external models.

However, in the context of complex multi-hop reasoning, pure self-correction is unverifiable and fundamentally limited, as LLMs often inherit the same hallucinations and biases that caused the original error. Consequently, models struggle to self-correct reasoning flaws without external ground-truth signals (Huang et al., 2023). This is further supported by Tyen et al. (2024), who identify mistake finding as the primary bottleneck, showing that unguided models consistently fail to rectify their own logical missteps.

Our distinction: SAFE enhances self-correction by introducing a dedicated, externally trained feedback model. Grounded in a rigorously verified dataset and a comprehensive error taxonomy, our external evaluator validates each atomic reasoning step to enforce a strictly verifiable sequence of grounded entities, providing more reliable supervision towards grounded reasoning.

3 Method

SAFE is structured into two phases: train-time and inference-time verification. During the train-time, we formalize the error taxonomy (Section 3.1) and systematically verify standard benchmarks (Section 3.2). For the inference-time, we introduce a dedicated feedback model, trained to dynamically verify reasoning trajectories (Section 3.3).

3.1 Taxonomy of Reasoning Errors

We formally define a valid reasoning trajectory as a strictly verifiable sequence of grounded entities. Unlike conventional CoT, this sequence operates exclusively as a traversal over a localized Knowledge Graph (𝒢\mathcal{G}), extending derived entities through explicitly grounded triples (eh​e​a​d,r,et​a​i​le_{head},r,e_{tail}). Every intermediate entity in the reasoning path serves as a verifiable anchor, effectively preventing logical hallucinations.

Toward this verification goal, we introduce a KG-grounded error taxonomy. As Section 2 contrasted, REVEAL Jacovi et al. (2024) is a similar post-hoc taxonomy without grounding, but we aim to provide a grounded verification per each entity. More specifically:

First, while REVEAL treats a reasoning step as a free-form sentence, we enforce strict atomic attribution, anchoring each step to exactly one evidence passage and one KG triple, which ensures strict grounding and enables precise step-level validation.

Second, whereas REVEAL’s post-hoc nature restricts it to static benchmarking, our taxonomy actively supports both training supervision and dynamic inference-time correction.

Specifically, we assign each atomic step exclusively to one error type from four mutually exclusive categories that we define: Procedural, Attribution, Logical, and Final Answer (Table 1). While existing benchmarks focus too much on answer correctness, sentence-level attribution, and logical errors, our distinction is investigating atomic-level procedural integrity.

According to our error taxonomy, reasoning errors are evaluated sequentially: Procedural errors capture invalid KG traversal patterns such as loops or disconnected paths. Once procedural validity is confirmed, Attribution errors detect missing or ungrounded evidence. Logical errors identify relational inferences unsupported by KG structure. Finally, Final Answer errors arise when the trajectory fails to reach the correct target node. This taxonomy provides a principled foundation for step-level supervision and real-time trajectory correction, enabling reasoning processes that are not only interpretable but strictly verifiable.

3.2 KG-grounded Benchmark Verification

Having formalized the atomic operations and error taxonomy required for strict grounding, we must ensure that the evaluation environment is also verifiable. When applying our defined KG constraints to standard large-scale benchmarks, we observe pervasive noise such as missing relations, ambiguous entity mappings, and incomplete supporting facts with spurious correlations. Such noise inherently hinders the formation of a valid sequence of grounded entities (see Appendix Figure 6 and Table 6). To systematically diagnose these deficiencies and guarantee that every evaluation instance possesses a grounded reasoning trajectory, we introduce a KG-grounded benchmark verification pipeline. Throughout this pipeline, we utilize gpt-oss-120b Agarwal et al. (2025) as our base LLM, selected for its state-of-the-art instruction-following capabilities and robust zero-shot relation extraction performance among open-weight models (exact prompts are detailed in Appendix A.9). The pipeline actively enforces our atomic grounding constraints through the following steps:

  1. 1.

    Triple Extraction: We prompt the LLM to extract atomic triples (eh​e​a​d,r,et​a​i​le_{head},r,e_{tail}) from the gold passages, conceptualizing the context as a localized knowledge graph.

  2. 2.

    Iterative Gleaning: To ensure no critical information is omitted, we perform up to two rounds of gleaning to capture valid triples that may have been overlooked during the initial extraction.

  3. 3.

    Entity Resolution: We identify and merge synonymous entities (e.g., “USA” and “United States”) to construct a cohesive and normalized knowledge graph.

  4. 4.

    Logical Path Discovery: We explicitly trace continuous relational paths within the localized KG to bridge the gap between the question entities and the ground truth answer.

  5. 5.

    Validation: An instance is systematically classified as noise and filtered out if no valid, continuous logical path can be established, confirming a fundamental break in the reasoning chain.

Appendix Figure 5 provides an overview of our benchmark verification pipeline, and the quantitative results of this rigorous diagnosis are summarized in Table 2. Our analysis reveals a substantial presence of noise across all examined benchmarks: 3%–14% of the data are corrupted by artifacts that prevent the formation of a valid sequence of grounded entities. By explicitly filtering out these ungrounded instances, we establish a verified, strictly grounded testing environment where the efficacy of our real-time feedback model can be measured solely on valid reasoning challenges.

3.3 Inference-time Feedback Model

Defining Step-Level Feedback.

To enforce the strict grounding paradigm during inference, we train a dedicated step-level feedback model that verifies reasoning trajectories and produces corrective guidance when violations occur. Formally, we model feedback generation as a conditional prediction task over reasoning prefixes. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the passages provided as context, and let a reasoning trajectory τ\tau be represented as a sequence of atomic steps:

τ=(s1,s2,…,st)\tau=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{t})

where each step sis_{i} corresponds to a KG operation (e.g., entity extraction or relational traversal) that must be explicitly grounded in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The feedback model FF receives the question qq, the passages 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and the current reasoning prefix s1:ts_{1:t} to predict:

(yt,dt,gt)=F(q,𝒫,s1:t)(y_{t},d_{t},g_{t})=F(q,\mathcal{P},s_{1:t})

where:

  • •

    yty_{t} denotes the specific error type (e.g., Unsupported, Logical Fallacy) assigned from the taxonomy defined in Section 3.1.

  • •

    dtd_{t} represents the natural language diagnosis, explicitly grounding why the step violates KG constraints based on 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

  • •

    gtg_{t} provides actionable guidance, directing the generator on how to correct the trajectory and construct a valid continuous path.

This formulation transforms feedback generation into a rigorous verification problem, where the model learns to detect deviations from valid grounding.

Building Training Data.

Training feedback model requires both verified reasoning trajectories and diverse failure modes. Using the verified environment (Section 3.2), we construct 3.9K ideal trajectories strictly grounded to the passages 𝒫\mathcal{P}. To provide robust negative supervision, we then synthesize 7.6K negative examples through taxonomy-guided error injection. Starting from these valid trajectories, a high-capacity teacher model (gpt-oss-120b) systematically perturbs individual reasoning steps by introducing violations aligned with our error taxonomy. This yields corrupted trajectories where the precise error location and type are known, enabling explicit step-level supervision.

While synthetic perturbations provide controlled coverage of error types, they may not fully capture the inherent path-finding failures and subtle misgrounding behaviors specific to the target model during actual inference. To bridge this distribution gap, we adopt an iterative refinement strategy: we first train an initial feedback model on the synthetic dataset, then conduct targeted failure analysis to identify recurring weaknesses (e.g., confusing lexically similar entities or failing at complex numerical comparisons). For each identified weakness, we leverage the teacher model to generate corrected step-level feedback labels, and reintegrate these hard cases into the training pool. Through this cycle of train →\rightarrow diagnose →\rightarrow augment, 848 hard cases are added to the training pool. This progressively closes the distribution gap between synthetic supervision and real inference-time failures, ultimately yielding a final dataset of 11.5K instances and a verifier robust to diverse and subtle KG deviations. We empirically validate the effectiveness of this refinement strategy in Section 5, where it consistently improves performance over training with synthetic data alone.

The overall error statistics of this complete training set are illustrated in Appendix Figure 7. Additional details, including the positional distribution of error steps and dataset statistics, are provided in Appendix A.5.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate our approach on three multi-hop QA benchmarks: 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022). To ensure rigorous evaluation, we apply our KG-grounded verification pipeline to the validation splits, extracting a sound pool from which we randomly sample 1,000 instances per benchmark (3,000 in total). Each question is evaluated in a constrained distractor setting provided with exactly 10 passages (including gold evidence). More details of data processing are provided in Appendix A.4.

Evaluation Metric.

Standard string-matching metrics, such as Exact Match (EM) and F1 scores, often underestimate model performance by failing to recognize semantic equivalence in surface-form variations or descriptive phrases. To ensure a more faithful assessment of the final output, we adopt an LLM-as-a-judge approach Li et al. (2025) using gpt-oss-120b to evaluate the semantic equivalence of the generated answers against the ground truth.

Models.

We evaluate our framework using a comprehensive range of models spanning multiple families and sizes. Specifically, we utilize Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), Qwen2.5-14B Qwen et al. (2025), Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma-3-12B (Team et al., 2025) as our reasoning generators.22 2 We use the instruct-tuned version when available. Our specialized inference-time feedback model is trained on the non-thinking version of Qwen3-8B, chosen specifically to prioritize training efficiency and architectural simplicity. For constructing the KG-grounded training data, we employ gpt-oss-120b Agarwal et al. (2025). This teacher model is responsible for generating ideal, strictly grounded reasoning paths, injecting taxonomy-based errors, and producing high-quality corrective feedback for the model-specific failures identified during our refinement process.

Evaluation Methods.

To rigorously evaluate SAFE, we compare it against both a recent specialized framework and fundamental reasoning methods. We employ TRACE (Fang et al., 2024) as our specialized baseline. Evaluated under the same context setting, it serves as a strong recent representative of utilizing KG chains for multi-hop QA, while relying on static pre-generation extraction rather than dynamic verification. For additional reference, we also report results from IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023), a retrieval-based multi-hop QA framework. Although IRCoT operates under a slightly different setting with iterative retrieval, its results are included for contextual reference alongside TRACE. To isolate the efficacy of our real-time feedback mechanism, we evaluate standard LLMs across three distinct methods:

  • •

    No Feedback: The model generates reasoning paths iteratively, producing a single atomic step per turn until reaching a final answer, without any verification.

  • •

    Self-Feedback: This baseline introduces an inference-time feedback loop (illustrated in Figure 1) where the generator evaluates its own grounding after each step, refining it if an error is detected. To ensure efficiency and prevent infinite loops, this process is constrained by a total step bound KK and a retry limit NN.

  • •

    SAFE: Operating under the same constraints, we substitute the self-evaluator with our trained feedback model. By decoupling evaluation from generation, we provide rigorous, taxonomy-based diagnostics and real-time corrective guidance.

Implementation Details.

We fine-tune the specialized feedback model using QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) on the Qwen3-8B (non-thinking) architecture for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and an effective batch size of 64. All experiments are conducted on 4×\times A6000 GPUs. During inference, we apply greedy decoding with a temperature of 0 for deterministic behavior. We set the maximum retry attempts (NN) to 3 and the overall reasoning steps (KK) to 10, which had the best balance between computational cost and performance (Appendix A.8). Exhaustive training details, including specific LoRA configurations, are provided in Appendix A.2.

4.2 Main Results

Table 3 presents the results across the three structurally verified multi-hop QA benchmarks. Even without any external verification (No Feedback), simply decomposing the reasoning process into atomic steps based on our KG-grounded taxonomy already yields higher performance than TRACE. This suggests that formatting multi-hop reasoning as a sequence of atomic operations inherently provides a solid baseline for generation.

In contrast, the Self-Feedback baseline demonstrates significant instability and frequently results in performance degradation. When models attempt to verify their own grounding, the total average accuracy drops from 76.7% to 75.2%. This vulnerability is most evident in Qwen 2.5 14B, where self-feedback drastically reduces accuracy from 80.7% to 75.1%. This phenomenon highlights a critical limitation: without reliable, external KG-grounded signals for error localization, LLMs struggle to diagnose their own failures, often hallucinating corrections or reinforcing ungrounded reasoning trajectories.

When equipped with our specialized feedback model (SAFE), performance improves substantially across all datasets and model families. By enforcing strict grounding constraints in real time, our method achieves an average accuracy improvement of 8.4 pp (Δ\Delta) over the best baselines, alongside a remarkable 11.2 pp surge in the rigorous EM metric (from 48.9% to 60.1%). Notably, SAFE demonstrates exceptional robustness on MuSiQue—the most challenging dataset requiring longer relational paths—boosting average accuracy by 11.1 pp (from 63.9% to 75.0%) and EM by 9.3 pp. Furthermore, it successfully breaks the performance ceiling on already high-performing benchmarks, pushing the average accuracy on both 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA beyond the 90% threshold.

Interestingly, despite variations in architecture and parameter scale, models tend to converge to a similar high-performance level (around 84%–85%) when augmented with SAFE. Overall, these findings demonstrate that enforcing strict grounding at the atomic step level, combined with our trained real-time feedback model, instantly corrects unverified trajectories, mitigates error propagation, narrows the performance gap across different LLMs, and provides a robust, model-agnostic strategy for verifiable multi-hop reasoning.

5 Analysis

Necessity of KG-Grounded Verification.

To empirically demonstrate the critical need for filtering unverifiable (flawed) data, we investigate its impact on the feedback model’s training phase. As shown in Table 4, we compared our standard feedback model, trained on the strictly verified dataset (11.5K), against a variant augmented with an additional 5.3K instances initially flagged as noise by our KG pipeline. Notably, these noise instances were generated using the identical data generation pipeline and format. However, their inclusion consistently degraded performance across all five models, resulting in an average accuracy drop of 4.0%. This substantial degradation underscores that training on ungrounded data introduces contradictory signals, ultimately compromising the feedback model’s ability to act as a reliable logical guardrail.

To verify that our pipeline targets genuine unverifiable reasoning traces rather than merely difficult queries, we manually inspected 150 flagged instances (50 per benchmark). We observed a remarkably low false positive rate of 2% (Appendix Table 6), confirming the pipeline’s precision. Among the truly flawed instances, 77% suffered from a lack of necessary evidence in the gold passages to deduce the answer. Appendix Table 6 presents representative unverifiable instances filtered by our pipeline.

Effect of Targeted Refinement.

To evaluate our strategy for bridging the distribution gap, we compare a model trained exclusively on synthetic errors against our final model incorporating analysis-driven targeted refinement (Appendix Table 12). This refinement consistently improves performance, yielding an average gain of 2.4 pp. The most substantial boost occurs on MuSiQue (+3.3 pp), demonstrating its ability to capture complex errors missed by purely synthetic data. Achieving this with only 848 hard cases (out of 11,515) confirms that selectively exposing the model to actual reasoning failures provides the robust negative supervision necessary for reliable inference-time rectification.

Cost-Accuracy: SAFE vs. Self-Feedback.

To investigate practical efficiency, Figure 2 compares the cost-accuracy trade-off of SAFE against the Self-Feedback baseline across varying reasoning budgets. As the retry limit increases, Self-Feedback suffers from a catastrophic cost explosion. It drives average LLM calls to nearly 60 without meaningful accuracy gains, because the lack of verifiable anchors frequently traps the model in flawed reasoning loops. In contrast, SAFE acts as a highly effective guardrail. By instantly rectifying ungrounded trajectories, it pushes accuracy beyond 84% with minimal computational overhead (<< 15 calls). This proves that strict grounding constraints are vastly more efficient than unguided self-correction. Furthermore, to mitigate the fundamental prefill overhead of iterative generation, our framework integrates Prefix KV caching (Kwon et al., 2023) and achieves an 89% reduction in redundant token processing. A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis, including the impact of hyperparameters KK and NN, is detailed in Appendix A.8.

Characterizing Reasoning Failures.

To investigate the nature of reasoning failures and the necessity of inference-time verification, we analyze the distribution of errors across categories and reasoning steps. As illustrated in Figure 3, our diagnostic results reveal two critical insights. First, procedural errors (e.g., Redundancy, Off-topic) constitute the majority (64.1%) of total failures. This suggests that LLM failures in multi-hop tasks are primarily driven by procedural breakdowns and repetitive reasoning loops rather than a simple lack of factual knowledge. Second, error occurrences are heavily concentrated in the early stages of reasoning; as shown in Figure 4, 59.0% of all errors occur within the first three steps. This early concentration indicates that initial reasoning errors create a flawed foundation, which inevitably propagates through the remaining steps to corrupt downstream reasoning. Consequently, these findings validate the core design of SAFE: inference-time verification is essential to correct these foundational flaws before they trigger cascading hallucinations.

Qualitative Analysis.

Our qualitative analysis (Appendix A.6) demonstrates that ungrounded self-feedback mechanisms frequently fail in multi-hop scenarios due to lexical overlap bias, logical leaps, and evaluator hallucination, compromising their overall reliability. In contrast, SAFE provides inference-time verification, enforcing strict grounding to anchor each step to verified facts and prevent contradictory loops.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced SAFE, a dynamic benchmarking framework that shifts multi-hop reasoning evaluation from static answer-matching to strictly verifiable grounding. During train-time, we formalized a rigorous error taxonomy and filtered ungrounded noise from standard benchmarks, providing a verified foundation for our feedback model. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our inference-time verification yields substantial performance gains while fundamentally enhancing the faithfulness of reasoning trajectories. Ultimately, our work proves that strict step-by-step grounding is significantly more efficient and reliable than ungrounded self-correction, setting a new standard for trustworthy and explainable AI evaluation.

7 Limitations

While we utilized a Knowledge Graph (KG) to ensure the quality of our verification pipeline, we acknowledge the potential for mislabeling due to inherent noise or incomplete coverage in the KG. To address this, rather than aggressively excluding instances that might contain valuable reasoning trajectories, we provide the original dataset with our feedback labels as an augmented resource. This non-destructive approach allows future researchers to audit, refine, or leverage the full context of the data while accounting for potential label noise in automated diagnostics.

Furthermore, the efficacy of the SAFE framework inherently relies on the reasoning generator’s instruction-following capabilities. We observed instances where, despite the feedback model successfully producing accurate diagnoses and explicit corrective guidance, the reasoning generator failed to effectively incorporate these instructions into its subsequent generation step. Such instruction-following failures can lead to uncorrected errors or repeated mistakes within the iterative loop. This highlights a dependency on the base language model’s capacity to adhere to complex, stepwise constraints, suggesting that future work must address the alignment between corrective feedback and the generator’s execution.

Finally, our current experimental setting operates under the assumption that all necessary gold passages are present within the provided context. In practical open-domain multi-hop scenarios, initial retrievals may omit crucial evidence, necessitating dynamic or iterative retrieval steps. The primary scope of this study, however, is deliberately focused on isolating and evaluating the model’s reasoning capabilities—specifically, how accurately it can synthesize and navigate multi-hop logic given that the required information is already available. Extending the SAFE framework to actively trigger external information retrieval when the feedback model diagnoses a missing premise remains a promising direction for future work.

Ethics Statement

This work introduces SAFE, a framework designed to enhance the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in multi-hop reasoning tasks through stepwise atomic feedback and error-correction. We acknowledge several ethical considerations and potential broader impacts associated with its development and deployment.

Transparency and Interpretability

A persistent ethical challenge with LLMs is their "black-box" nature, which obscures the rationale behind generated answers. SAFE directly addresses this opacity by decomposing the complex multi-hop reasoning process into a fine-grained, stepwise atomic framework. This design transforms an otherwise opaque generation process into an inherently explainable system. By isolating each reasoning step and its corresponding feedback, researchers and practitioners can rigorously analyze the exact distribution of reasoning failures. This granular transparency not only facilitates precise, targeted error-correction but also promotes essential trust, accountability, and auditing capabilities in AI decision-making.

Computational Efficiency and Environmental Impact

Iterative reasoning and error-correction frameworks traditionally incur significant computational overhead due to repeated generation steps. However, SAFE explicitly mitigates this issue by employing efficient KV caching mechanisms, rendering the additional inference-time cost negligible compared to standard single-pass generation. By achieving robust multi-hop reasoning without heavily inflating computational demands, our approach aligns with the growing ethical need for sustainable and energy-efficient AI.

Bias and Fairness

The performance and behavior of SAFE inherently depend on the underlying pre-trained LLMs and the external knowledge corpora (e.g., retrieved Wikipedia passages) used for reasoning. These base models and datasets may contain historical, cultural, or demographic biases. While our error-correction taxonomy meticulously targets procedural, logical, and attribution errors, it is not explicitly designed to detect or mitigate social biases. Users must remain cautious, as the system might inadvertently reproduce or amplify existing biases present in the source material.

AI Usage

AI-based tools were used for grammar correction and language refinement. The authors take full responsibility for all scientific content, including the methodology, experiments, and conclusions.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Overview

This appendix provides supplementary materials, extended analyses, and examples to support the findings presented in the main text. The contents are organized as follows:

  • •

    Section A.2 provides comprehensive implementation details of the feedback model training, including hyperparameters and hardware specifications to facilitate full reproducibility.

  • •

    Section A.3 provides qualitative examples of our KG-grounded verification process, illustrating instances of false positives and inherent benchmark noise that our pipeline successfully identifies (see Table 6, Table 6, and Figure 6).

  • •

    Section A.4 details the preprocessing steps for our multi-hop evaluation benchmarks to ensure rigorous and unbiased assessment.

  • •

    Section A.5 provides details of our training dataset, offering data examples, error positions, and data statistics (detailed in Figure 8, Figure 9, and Table 7).

  • •

    Section A.6 presents a rigorous qualitative case study. By comparing our framework against a self-feedback baseline, we demonstrate our model’s robustness against common multi-hop failure modes, including lexical distractors, premature attribution, and evaluator-induced reasoning collapse (illustrated in Table 9, Table 10, and Table 11).

  • •

    Section A.7 details an ablation study comparing the performance impact of utilizing synthetic data only versus the full dataset (refer to Table 12).

  • •

    Section A.8 provides a detailed efficiency analysis, including the sensitivity of reasoning performance to hyperparameters KK (max steps) and NN (max retries), alongside details of Prefix KV caching.

  • •

    Section A.9 comprehensively lists all prompts utilized throughout our pipeline—including reasoning generation, evaluation, error injection, and knowledge graph construction—to ensure full transparency and reproducibility. (see Figure 15 to 23)

A.2 Implementation Details of the Training

As mentioned in Section 4.1, we fine-tune the feedback model using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) with QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023). We set the LoRA rank to r=64r=64, scaling factor α=128\alpha=128, and dropout to 0.050.05, applying LoRA to all linear modules, including the attention projections (qq, kk, vv, o​_​p​r​o​jo\_proj) and MLP layers (g​a​t​egate, u​pup, and d​o​w​n​_​p​r​o​jdown\_proj). For optimization, we use the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) and a cosine scheduler with a warmup ratio of 0.030.03.

A.3 KG-driven Noise Filtering: Examples

False Positive Examples

Table 6 presents qualitative examples of false positives encountered during our KG-driven noise filtering process. In this context, a false positive refers to a valid, well-structured multi-hop query that our pipeline incorrectly flagged as noise.

As illustrated by the three representative cases, the provided gold passages actually contain all the necessary informational components to successfully complete the required reasoning chains. For instance, the queries require cross-referencing directors’ ages, matching a specific birth date to a TV show judge, or tracing a newspaper’s sponsorship to its base city. In all of these instances, the textual evidence is clear, self-contained, and fully supports an unambiguous answer.

Crucially, these examples demonstrate that misclassifications occur even on standard, highly logical reasoning paths. They are not exclusively concentrated on exceptionally convoluted or poorly phrased queries. This observation is significant because it indicates that while our filtering mechanism is rigorous, it does not systematically bias the dataset against reasoning difficulty or penalize complex logical structures. Consequently, the filtered dataset accurately preserves the depth of reasoning required for a robust evaluation of multi-hop QA systems.

Noise Examples

In contrast to the false positives discussed previously, Table 6 and Figure 6 underscore the critical need for our KG-driven filtering pipeline by exposing the inherent noise prevalent in standard multi-hop benchmarks. We categorize these dataset flaws into distinct failure modes that fundamentally compromise reasoning evaluation.

First, benchmarks frequently suffer from insufficient context (illustrated in Table 6 and the bottom of Figure 6). In such cases, the provided gold passages lack the necessary evidence to complete the logical chain—for instance, detailing a composer’s year of death but omitting the location.

Furthermore, datasets occasionally suffer from entity confusion. Table 6 illustrates an instance where two distinct historical figures (Lorenzo Costa the Elder and the Younger) are incorrectly conflated to force a reasoning path. Even more problematic are incorrect ground-truth labels that directly contradict the provided text (see the top of Figure 6), such as identifying a director’s nationality as Lebanese when the gold passage explicitly states she is Palestinian. Additionally, Figure 6 (middle) highlights queries that are inherently ambiguous and lack a single definitive answer.

By systematically filtering out these unanswerable, contradictory, and ambiguous instances, our framework ensures that models are evaluated strictly on their atomic reasoning capabilities, rather than their propensity to guess, hallucinate, or rely on parametric memorization.

A.4 Evaluation Dataset Preprocessing Details

For our evaluation, we standardize the context length across all benchmarks to exactly 10 passages per question. For 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA, we directly utilize the 10 passages provided in their standard distractor settings. Since MuSiQue originally provides 20 passages per instance, we retain all gold supporting passages and randomly sample from the remaining distractors to strictly maintain the 10-passage constraint. Finally, to prevent language models from exploiting positional shortcuts, the sequence of the provided passages is randomly shuffled for every instance across all three datasets.

A.5 Training Dataset

This section outlines the structure, composition, and statistical distribution of the dataset used to train our specialized feedback model.

Figure 8 illustrates a representative training instance. Unlike traditional post-hoc evaluation datasets, our training data is explicitly structured to support atomic, step-level verification during inference. Each instance provides the model with the full context: the question, a set of retrieved passages, the trajectory of previous reasoning steps, and the current step under evaluation. The target output is formulated as a structured feedback triplet comprising the specific Error Type, a detailed Diagnosis explaining the logical or factual flaw, and actionable Guidance for real-time correction or next step generation.

Table 7 details the quantitative statistics of our constructed dataset across three standard multi-hop benchmarks: 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue. The dataset comprises a total of 11,515 step-level feedback instances derived from 5,060 unique questions. Because our framework evaluates reasoning iteratively, a single unique question inherently yields multiple training data points. This one-to-many mapping allows the model to learn a diverse array of valid and invalid logical transitions within a single reasoning trajectory.

Finally, Figure 9 presents the positional distribution of error steps across the reasoning chains. For a step-level verification system to be robust, it must not overfit to errors that exclusively occur at the beginning or the end of a reasoning path. As demonstrated in the figure, our dataset maintains a balanced coverage of errors across all reasoning stages. This balanced distribution ensures that the trained feedback model remains strictly position-agnostic, equipping it to reliably detect and diagnose reasoning failures at any arbitrary point during inference.

A.6 Qualitative Analysis: Case Study

In this section, we provide a qualitative analysis by examining a representative instance where the self-feedback baseline fails, whereas our proposed framework successfully arrives at the correct answer. This comparison highlights the effectiveness of our methodology in accurately detecting and rectifying reasoning errors in inference-time, faithfully fulfilling query requirements, and ensuring the precise utilization of information from the provided passages.

Table 9 demonstrates our model’s robustness against lexical distractors. While the self-feedback baseline is misled by the term "Eden" in Passage 1 due to lexical overlap bias, our model correctly identifies the factual contradiction using Passage 10. By distinguishing the hamlet "Eden" from the entity "Lake Eden," our framework ensures the reasoning remains grounded in the correct evidence. This highlights its superior ability in entity disambiguation and filtering irrelevant context.

Furthermore, our approach addresses structural logic gaps that extend beyond surface-level terminology. As illustrated in Table 10, the self-feedback exhibits a typical failure mode in multi-hop reasoning, characterized by Premature Attribution. Specifically, in Step 1, the generator jumps directly to extracting a death date without first establishing the link between the film and the director. This initial error triggers a cascade of implicit assumptions, eventually causing the model to lose track of the query’s primary constraint—identifying a film title. Consequently, it outputs the director’s name instead, failing the task despite having access to all relevant passages.

In contrast, our feedback model prevents this cascading error by monitoring the reasoning trace at each step to identify missing links and forcing real-time refinement. By intervening as early as Step 1, the model ensures that each subsequent step is built on a verified foundation. Moreover, by providing explicit guidance in the final stages—specifying that the final answer must be a <film_title>—our framework ensures that the entire reasoning process remains strictly aligned with the question’s specific requirements.

Finally, beyond structural logic gaps, self-feedback mechanisms are highly susceptible to evaluator-induced failures that lead to complete reasoning collapse. As detailed in Table 11, the baseline model exhibits a catastrophic breakdown driven by two critical errors. First, the evaluator suffers from target drift: rather than maintaining focus on the entity requested by the query (the second largest city, Tucson), it incorrectly shifts the generator’s objective to an irrelevant target (Phoenix). Second, upon failing to find the population of Phoenix in the provided text, the evaluator commits a hallucination by explicitly instructing the generator to reference external sources.

A.7 Ablation: Synthetic only vs. Full dataset

To evaluate the effectiveness of our training data curation strategy, we conducted an ablation study comparing the performance of feedback models trained strictly on synthetically generated error-injected data (“Synthetic Only”) against models trained on the full dataset, which incorporates our analysis-driven refinement strategy (“Refined”). The results, spanning various model architectures and parameter sizes, are detailed in Table 12.

Overall, integrating the refined data yields a consistent and noticeable performance improvement, demonstrating a +2.4 pp gain on average across all evaluated models. Notably, the most significant enhancements are observed on MuSiQue, the most challenging dataset in our benchmark, which sees an average improvement of +3.3 pp. This indicates that the refined training data provides crucial supervisory signals for diagnosing complex, deeply entangled reasoning errors that purely programmatic synthetic error injection fails to capture adequately.

When analyzing individual models, the impact of the full dataset is most pronounced in the Llama 3.1 8B model, which exhibits a substantial average performance jump of +6.3 pp, including a remarkable +8.0 pp increase on MuSiQue. Furthermore, even for highly capable larger models such as Gemma 3 12B, the refined data contributes a robust +2.6 pp average improvement. While the gains are more marginal for models like Qwen 2.5 14B (+0.4 pp average) and there is a negligible regression for Qwen 3 4B on HotpotQA (-0.2 pp), the overarching trend overwhelmingly validates our dataset construction approach.

Ultimately, this ablation confirms that relying solely on synthetic error injection is insufficient for training a highly robust feedback model. The inclusion of the full, analysis-driven refined dataset is essential for helping the model generalize across diverse and subtle failure modes, thereby maximizing the efficacy of inference-time reasoning correction.

A.8 Efficiency

Cost-accuracy Trade-off

To investigate the impact of exploration budget and correction limits on overall performance, we conducted an ablation study varying max_steps KK and max_retries NN. As illustrated in Figure 10, accuracy generally improves with larger steps and more retries, demonstrating the effectiveness of allowing the model sufficient room to refine its outputs. However, we observe a clear plateau in performance; increasing NN beyond 3 yields marginal gains or even slight degradations. While the highest accuracy (84.71%) is achieved at KK=13 and NN=3, this setting demands higher computational cost. Therefore, we select KK=10 and NN=3 (84.40%) as our optimal configuration. This spot strikes the best balance between computational cost and performance, achieving near-maximum accuracy while maintaining a highly efficient step budget.

KV Caching

A primary concern with iterative inference-time feedback mechanisms is the potential for a substantial escalation in computational cost and latency. In multi-hop QA, the vast majority of the computational burden arises from the initial prefill stage, which involves processing lengthy system instructions, retrieved documents, and the original query.

As shown in Table 8, our framework effectively mitigates this overhead through Prefix KV caching Kwon et al. (2023). To minimize redundant computation, both the reasoning generator and the feedback model independently cache the representations of these static prefixes. Crucially, as the stepwise generation progresses, previously verified reasoning steps are iteratively appended to this cached context. Consequently, subsequent reasoning steps and targeted feedback loops only incur the marginal cost of computing attention for the newly generated tokens. Empirical results, aggregated from a total of 3,000 samples across three benchmarks, demonstrate an impressive overall prefill token saving ratio of 89.0%, confirming the high efficiency of our approach.

A.9 Prompts

In this section, we provide the complete set of prompt templates utilized throughout our framework to ensure full transparency and reproducibility. For clarity, the prompts are grouped according to their specific roles within our pipeline:

  • •

    Inference and Evaluation: Includes templates for step-by-step reasoning generation (Figure 11), inference-time verification and feedback (Figure 12), and the extraction of the final answer (Figure 13). It also details the prompt used for the automated LLM judge to accurately score the final predicted answers against the ground truth (Figure 14).

  • •

    Training Data Construction: Contains the specialized prompts used to tailor initial query decomposition and planning for different benchmark structures: 2WikiMultiHopQA (Figure 15), HotpotQA (Figure 16), and MuSiQue (Figure 17). It also includes the prompts used to synthesize our training dataset by first generating correct, gold-standard reasoning chains (Figure 18) and subsequently perturbing them with targeted taxonomy-based error injection (Figure 19).

  • •

    KG-driven Noise Filtering: Details the series of prompts utilized in our knowledge graph pipeline to clean benchmark data. This includes extracting triples (Figure 20 and 21), matching synonymous or coreferent terms (Figure 22), and verifying the logical connectivity of the reasoning chain (Figure 23).
